Vibrissae (whiskers) of harbor seals and elephant seals possess undulations along their length.
Harbor seal vibrissae have been shown to reduce vortex-induced vibrations and drag compared to appropriately scaled cylinders and ellipses.
The researchers obtained seal whisker samples from the Marine Mammal Center in California and used CT scanning, microscopy, and 3D scanning to characterize the whisker geometries.
The computational fluid dynamics simulations were conducted using the NASA in-house Unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes code, Glenn-HT, with the SST-transition enabled two-equation model.
The baseline untreated variable speed power turbine (VSPT) blade showed separation at negative and high positive incidence angles.
The seal-inspired blades were created by sweeping the VSPT airfoil section through sinusoidal profiles with varying pitch and amplitude to match the seal whisker characteristics.
The seal blades showed a reduction in total pressure loss coefficient of up to 50% compared to the untreated baseline blade at a Reynolds number of 100,000.
Hotwire surveys in the wake of the seal-inspired blades showed a reduction in broadband frequency content and turbulence intensity.
The seal blades were found to be insensitive to incidence angle, maintaining improved performance over the untreated blade at angles ranging from -37 to +10 degrees.
The researchers estimated a potential fuel burn reduction of approximately 5% for a fixed-wing aircraft using the seal-inspired turbine blades.
Other biological inspirations reviewed in the study included owl wings, whale tubercles, dragonfly wings, cactus and palm tree trunks, and sailfish skin.
The computational fluid dynamics simulations were validated against experimental data from the NASA CW-22 wind tunnel facility for the baseline untreated turbine blade.
The researchers hypothesized that the seal-inspired undulations could delay or mitigate separation, thin the boundary layer, and modify the wake structure to reduce drag and noise.
Future work identified by the researchers includes investigating the effect of undulation sweep along the chord and the potential for acoustic attenuation.

The researchers conducted the study on a variable speed power turbine (VSPT) blade due to its large thickness-to-chord ratio and the existence of separation, which provided a suitable case for initial testing of the concept.
